```{r setup, include = FALSE}
if(!file.exists("DATA")){dir.create("DATA")}

knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(rconvertu)
library(forecast)

number_fmt  <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")  # ancillary function
percent_fmt <- function(x, digits = 2) {              # ancillary function
  paste0(format(round(100 * x, digits), nsmall = digits), "%")
}
```

## Introduction

The COVID-19 pandemic affected every country in the world. To monitor its
course, between January 2020 and March 2023, the Center for Systems Science and
Engineering (hereafter abbreviated as CSSE) at Johns Hopkins University
maintained a dataset compiled from data retrieved from  national health
authorities, downloadable from a single GitHub repository [1], [2]. This brief
report presents the main findings from its global time series of cumulative
confirmed cases and deaths by country and answers three research questions:
(1) what were the long-term trends of cumulative cases, deaths, and, above all,
the mortality rate (total deaths to total cases, i.e., the case fatality rate)
for the world as a whole (aggregated to monthly frequency to employ time-series
models), (2) were cases, deaths, and the mortality rate distributed uniformly
across countries, and (3) which (preferably, automatically selected) ARIMA model
describes the monthly world series and what does it predict for the subsequent
12 months. Each question is complemented with a formal statistical hypothesis
(or model for the Auto-ARIMA) tested at the standard 5% significance level
($\alpha=0.05$):

- **H1**. Monthly cumulative cases, deaths, and the mortality rate have a
  statistically significant linear trend, i.e., $\beta_1 \neq 0$ in
  $y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t$, at both world (total of all countries) and
  individual country level.

- **H2**. Across countries, cases and deaths are distributed uniformly, and
  the mortality rate is uniform (i.e., deaths are distributed proportionally
  to cases), under a built-in Pearson's $\chi^2$ goodness-of-fit test.

- **H3**. The monthly world time series are adequately described and afterward
  predicted (for at least the subsequent 12 months) by an
  $ARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)_{12}$ process, selected automatically by the
  Hyndman-Khandakar algorithm [3], i.e., the model residuals are white noise
  under the Ljung-Box test.

To compile this report, R packages `tidyverse`, `lubridate`, `rconvertu`
(the author's package converting between country names and ISO 3166-1 alpha-3,
alpha-2, and numeric codes using regular expressions), `ggplot2`, and
`forecast` were employed, with all R code embedded into the R Markdown document
to ensure its reproducibility. The CSV datasets, downloaded from the CSSE GitHub
repository, are accessed in the folder `./DATA/` as
`time_series_covid19_confirmed_global.csv` and
`time_series_covid19_deaths_global.csv` (the detailed US files are ignored).
The report is subdivided into five parts: data description and processing,
time trends, cross-country structure, (ARIMA) time-series model with a
12-month forecast, and potential bias.

## Data Description and Processing

```{r hidden1, include = FALSE}
RAW_CASES   <- read_csv('./DATA/time_series_covid19_confirmed_global.csv')
RAW_DEATHS  <- read_csv('./DATA/time_series_covid19_deaths_global.csv')
n_rows      <- nrow(RAW_CASES)
n_cols      <- ncol(RAW_CASES)
n_na        <- sum(is.na(RAW_CASES)) + sum(is.na(RAW_DEATHS))
n_countries <- n_distinct(RAW_CASES$`Country/Region`, na.rm = TRUE)
n_provinces <- sum(!is.na(RAW_CASES$`Province/State`))
dates       <- mdy(names(RAW_CASES)[-(1:4)])
t_min       <- format(min(dates, na.rm = TRUE), "%B %d, %Y")
t_max       <- format(max(dates, na.rm = TRUE), "%B %d, %Y")
```

The raw (unprocessed) dataset consists of two CSV files (confirmed cumulative
cases and deaths), each with `r number_fmt(n_rows)` rows and
`r number_fmt(n_cols)` columns, i.e., `r n_countries` countries and
`r n_provinces` provinces or territories thereof, with one row per territorial
unit and one column per day between `r t_min` and `r t_max` (i.e., the dataset
is in a wide format). Given that the data comprise `r number_fmt(n_na)` missing
values (all in `Province/State`), daily cumulative counts (which are too
detailed for the intended time-series analysis), unused columns (`Lat`, `Long`),
non-ISO 3166-1 country names (e.g., "US", "Korea, South", or "Taiwan*"), and
minor value inconsistencies (e.g., "Congo (Brazzaville)" and "West Bank and
Gaza" must be recoded for the ISO 3166-1 conversion), the raw dataset required
several preprocessing steps -- employing `tidyverse`'s `pivot_longer()`,
`full_join()`, `select()`, `mutate()`, `group_by()`, `summarize()`, and
`slice_max()` functions, alongside `rconvertu`'s `convertu()` for ISO 3166-1
alpha-3 codes (`ISO3`) and English names (`NAME_EN`) -- to obtain a modified
panel tibble `COVID` in a long format (month-end cumulative values) and the
world totals `WORLD` (consult the R code field below).

```{r tidy, echo = TRUE, results = 'hide'}
COVID <- read_csv('./DATA/time_series_covid19_confirmed_global.csv')         %>%
         pivot_longer(-(1:4), names_to = "DATE", values_to = "CASES")        %>%
         full_join(
         read_csv('./DATA/time_series_covid19_deaths_global.csv')            %>%
         pivot_longer(-(1:4), names_to = "DATE", values_to = "DEATHS")       %>%
         select(-c(Lat, Long)),
         by = c("Province/State", "Country/Region", "DATE"))                 %>%
         select(  COUNTRY   = `Country/Region`, DATE, CASES, DEATHS)         %>%
         mutate(  COUNTRY   = recode(COUNTRY,
                              "Congo (Brazzaville)" = "Republic of the Congo",
                              "West Bank and Gaza"  = "Palestine"),
                  DATE      = mdy(DATE),
                  MONTH     = floor_date(DATE, "month"))                     %>%
         group_by(COUNTRY, MONTH, DATE)                                      %>%
                  summarize(CASES     = sum(CASES,  na.rm = TRUE),
                            DEATHS    = sum(DEATHS, na.rm = TRUE),
                            .groups   = "drop")                              %>%
         group_by(COUNTRY, MONTH)                                            %>%
                  slice_max(DATE, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)                  %>%
         group_by(COUNTRY)                                                   %>%
         mutate(  ISO3      = convertu(to = "iso3",    text = first(COUNTRY)),
                  NAME_EN   = convertu(to = "name_en", text = first(COUNTRY)),
                  ISO3      = factor(if_else(ISO3 == COUNTRY, NA, ISO3)),
                  MORTALITY = if_else(CASES > 0, DEATHS / CASES, NA))        %>%
         ungroup()                                                           %>%
         filter(  !is.na(ISO3))                                              %>%
         select(  ISO3, NAME_EN, MONTH, CASES, DEATHS, MORTALITY)            %>%
         arrange( ISO3, MONTH)

WORLD <- COVID                                                               %>%
         group_by(MONTH)                                                     %>%
                  summarize(CASES     = sum(CASES,  na.rm = TRUE),
                            DEATHS    = sum(DEATHS, na.rm = TRUE),
                            .groups   = "drop")                              %>%
         mutate(  MORTALITY = DEATHS / CASES)
```

```{r hidden2, include = FALSE}
n_rows        <- nrow(COVID)
n_cols        <- ncol(COVID)
n_na_tidy     <- sum( is.na(COVID))
n_iso3        <- n_distinct(COVID$ISO3)
m_min         <- format(min(COVID$MONTH, na.rm = TRUE), "%B %Y")
m_max         <- format(max(COVID$MONTH, na.rm = TRUE), "%B %Y")
dropped       <- RAW_CASES                                                   %>%
                 distinct(COUNTRY = `Country/Region`)                        %>%
                 mutate(ISO3 = convertu(to = "iso3", text = recode(COUNTRY,
                              "Congo (Brazzaville)" = "Republic of the Congo",
                              "West Bank and Gaza"  = "Palestine")))         %>%
                 filter(ISO3 == COUNTRY)                                     %>%
                 pull(COUNTRY)
LATEST        <- COVID                                                       %>%
                 filter(MONTH == max(MONTH))
total_cases   <- sum(LATEST$CASES,  na.rm = TRUE)
total_deaths  <- sum(LATEST$DEATHS, na.rm = TRUE)
mortality     <- total_deaths / total_cases
top           <- function(x, n = 3, min_cases = 0) {
  LATEST                                                                     %>%
  filter(CASES >= min_cases)                                                 %>%
  slice_max(order_by = {{x}}, n = n, with_ties = FALSE)                      %>%
  pull(NAME_EN)                                                              %>%
  paste(collapse = ", ")
}
```

The obtained panel tibble `COVID` consists of `r number_fmt(n_rows)` rows
(`r n_iso3` countries $\times$ `r n_distinct(COVID$MONTH)` months) and
`r n_cols` columns, with `r number_fmt(n_na_tidy)` missing values
(`MORTALITY` is undefined without confirmed cases); `r length(dropped)` units
without an ISO 3166-1 code (`r paste(dropped, collapse = ", ")`) were
dropped. Between `r m_min` and `r m_max`,
**`r number_fmt(total_cases)` confirmed cases** and
**`r number_fmt(total_deaths)` deaths** were reported, i.e., a **mortality
rate of `r percent_fmt(mortality)`**, with the most cases and deaths in
**`r top(DEATHS, n = 1)`**, and the highest mortality rate (among countries with
over 1,000 cases) in **`r top(MORTALITY, n = 1, min_cases = 1000)`**. The
`summary()` output is below.

```{r summary, echo = TRUE}
summary(COVID)
```

## Analysis of Time Trends

```{r hidden3, include = FALSE}
SLOPES   <- COVID                                                            %>%
            filter(!is.na(MORTALITY))                                        %>%
            arrange(ISO3, MONTH)                                             %>%
            group_by(ISO3)                                                   %>%
            filter(n() >= 12)                                                %>%
            summarize(MODEL = list(summary(lm(100 * MORTALITY ~
                                               seq_along(MONTH)))),
                      .groups = "drop")                                      %>%
            transmute(
              Slope   = sapply(MODEL, \(m) m$coefficients[2, 1]),
              P       = sapply(MODEL, \(m) m$coefficients[2, 4])
            )
n_slopes <- nrow(SLOPES)
n_neg    <- sum(SLOPES$P < 0.05 & SLOPES$Slope < 0)
n_pos    <- sum(SLOPES$P < 0.05 & SLOPES$Slope > 0)
peak     <- WORLD                                                            %>%
            slice_max(MORTALITY, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
slope_m  <- abs(coef(lm(100 * MORTALITY ~ seq_along(MONTH), WORLD))[2])
```

Aggregated monthly data show an increasing (cumulative) number
of cases and deaths worldwide, with the steepest increase in cases during the
so-called Omicron wave in early 2022 (see Figure 1). The mortality rate, on the
contrary, peaked at `r percent_fmt(peak$MORTALITY)` in
`r format(peak$MONTH, "%B %Y")`, when testing was scarce and limited to
severe cases only, and then declined steadily towards `r percent_fmt(mortality)`
in `r m_max` due to advances in mitigation (among other, vaccine roll-out), 
reducing the disease to milder variants. Both cumulative curves also
flattened in late 2022 and early 2023, when many countries scaled down reporting
(the CSSE's last dataset update was on March 10, 2023).

```{r figure1, echo = TRUE, fig.height = 3, fig.pos = "H"}
ggplot(WORLD                                                                 %>%
       transmute(MONTH, Cases = CASES, Deaths = DEATHS,
                `Mortality rate (%)` = 100 * MORTALITY)                      %>%
       pivot_longer(-MONTH, names_to = "SERIES", values_to = "VALUE")        %>%
       mutate(SERIES = factor(SERIES, levels = c("Cases", "Deaths",
                                                 "Mortality rate (%)"))),
       aes(x = MONTH, y = VALUE))                                              +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7)                                                   +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, linewidth = 0.5, color = "red")  +
  facet_wrap(~SERIES, scales = "free_y", axes = "all_x",
                                         axis.labels = "all_x")                +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma)                                   +
  labs(
    title = paste0("Figure 1. Cases, deaths, and mortality rate, ",
                   format(min(WORLD$MONTH), "%b %Y"), "-",
                   format(max(WORLD$MONTH), "%b %Y")),
    x = "Month",
    y = "Cumulative value (world)"
  )                                                                            +
  theme_minimal()
```

The formal statistical test of **H1** is tied to coefficients $\beta_1$ from
three linear regression models `lm(VALUE ~ MONTH SEQUENCE)`, i.e., for the
cumulative cases, deaths, and the mortality rate of the world as a whole,
with the `MONTH` encoded with the help of `seq_along()` into a time-series
sequence. Since the CSSE data contain no regional (continental) aggregates,
the same model was also estimated for the mortality rate of each of the
`r n_slopes` countries with at least 12 months of data: the slope is
significantly negative for `r n_neg`, significantly positive for `r n_pos`,
and insignificant for `r n_slopes - n_neg - n_pos` countries, i.e., the
declining world trend is shared by a majority
(`r round(100 * n_neg / n_slopes)`%) of countries. Table 1 comprises the
slopes, their standard errors, the two-sided p-values, and the $R^2$ of the
fit: all three coefficients are non-zero at the 5% significance level
($\alpha=0.05$), with the mortality rate declining on average by
`r round(slope_m, 3)` percentage points per month. However, the high $R^2$
values of cumulative series are typical of integrated (non-stationary)
processes, i.e., potential unit roots to be addressed by an (S)ARIMA model.

```{r table1, echo = TRUE}
WORLD                                                                        %>%
transmute(MONTH, Cases = CASES, Deaths = DEATHS,
          `Mortality rate (%)` = 100 * MORTALITY)                            %>%
pivot_longer(-MONTH, names_to = "SERIES", values_to = "VALUE")               %>%
mutate(  SERIES = factor(SERIES, levels = c("Cases", "Deaths",
                                            "Mortality rate (%)")))          %>%
 arrange(SERIES, MONTH)                                                      %>%
group_by(SERIES)                                                             %>%
         summarize(MODEL = list(summary(lm(VALUE ~ seq_along(MONTH)))))      %>%
transmute(
         Series  = SERIES,
         Slope   = sapply(MODEL, \(m) m$coefficients[2, 1]),
         SE      = sapply(MODEL, \(m) m$coefficients[2, 2]),
         P       = sapply(MODEL, \(m) m$coefficients[2, 4]),
         R2      = sapply(MODEL, \(m) m$r.squared)
)                                                                            %>%
mutate(P = scales::pvalue(P, accuracy = 0.001))                              %>%
knitr::kable(digits  = 3, format.args = list(big.mark = ",",
                                             scientific = FALSE),
             caption = "Linear trends in world cases, deaths, and mortality")
```

## Analysis of Cross-Country Structure

Figure 2 demonstrates the distribution of cases, deaths, and the mortality
rate by country (labeled with ISO 3166-1 alpha-3 codes) as of `r m_max`.
Namely, the three countries with the most cases are **`r top(CASES)`**, with
the most deaths **`r top(DEATHS)`**, and with the highest mortality rate
(among countries with over 1,000 cases, which excludes a handful of
micro-states with implausible ratios) **`r top(MORTALITY, min_cases = 1000)`**.
Whereas the first two rankings are dominated by populous countries, the third one
comprises mostly low-income or conflict-affected countries, i.e., strongly
indicating a non-uniform distribution of the examined COVID data.

```{r figure2, echo = TRUE, fig.height = 3.6, fig.pos = "H"}
ggplot(LATEST                                                                %>%
       transmute(ISO3, Cases = CASES, Deaths = DEATHS,
                 `Mortality rate (%)` = if_else(CASES >= 1000,
                                                100 * MORTALITY, NA))        %>%
       pivot_longer(-ISO3,  names_to  = "SERIES", values_to = "VALUE")       %>%
       filter(!is.na(VALUE))                                                 %>%
       mutate(SERIES = factor(SERIES, levels = c("Cases", "Deaths",
                                                 "Mortality rate (%)")))     %>%
       group_by(SERIES)                                                      %>%
                slice_max(order_by = VALUE, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE)       %>%
       ungroup(),
       aes(x = reorder(paste(ISO3, SERIES, sep = "|"), VALUE), y = VALUE))     +
  geom_col(width = 0.7)                                                        +
  coord_flip()                                                                 +
  facet_wrap(~ SERIES, scales = "free", axes        = "all_x",
                                        axis.labels = "all_x")                 +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = \(x) str_remove(x, "\\|.*$"))                      +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_number(
                              scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale()))          +
  labs(
    title = paste0("Figure 2. Top ten countries (ISO 3166-1 codes), ",
                   format(max(COVID$MONTH), "%b %Y")),
    x = "Country (ISO3)",
    y = "Cumulative value"
  )                                                                            +
  theme_minimal()
```

The formal statistical test of **H2** is based on Pearson's chi-square
goodness-of-fit test `chisq.test()` applied to three distributions across
countries as of `r m_max`, i.e., for the world as a whole (regional
aggregates being absent from the data). For cases and deaths, the null
hypothesis assumes a uniform distribution across the $k$ countries
($H_0: p_1 = p_2 = \cdots = p_k = 1/k$); for the mortality rate, it assumes
deaths distributed proportionally to cases
($H_0: p_i = \text{CASES}_i / \sum_{j=1}^{k} \text{CASES}_j$), i.e., an
identical mortality rate in every country, with a p-value precision of
$0.001$. Table 2 comprises the $\chi^2$ statistics, degrees of freedom, and
upper-tail p-values. $H_0$ is rejected in all cases at the 5% significance
level ($\alpha=0.05$), confirming a statistically significant non-uniform
distribution across countries, which may reflect variations in population
size, age structure, testing capacity, healthcare quality, reporting
standards, etc. -- i.e., potential relationships that require further
investigation.

```{r table2, echo = TRUE}
LATEST                                                                       %>%
summarize(
         Cases            = list(chisq.test(CASES)),
         Deaths           = list(chisq.test(DEATHS)),
        `Mortality rate`  = list(chisq.test(DEATHS, p = CASES / sum(CASES)))
)                                                                            %>%
pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "SERIES", values_to = "TEST")          %>%
transmute(
         Series  = SERIES,
         Chi2    = sapply(TEST, \(m) unname(m$statistic)),
         DF      = sapply(TEST, \(m) unname(m$parameter)),
         P       = sapply(TEST, \(m) m$p.value)
)                                                                            %>%
mutate(P = scales::pvalue(P, accuracy = 0.001))                              %>%
knitr::kable(digits  = 3, format.args = list(big.mark = ",",
                                             scientific = FALSE),
             caption = "Pearson chi-square tests of uniform distribution")
```

## Time-Series Model and Forecast

In order to describe the dynamics of the three monthly world series and to
forecast their values for the 12 months following `r m_max` -- which may provide
valuable insights for public health authorities in anticipating the burden of
the disease -- the following seasonal autoregressive integrated moving average
model, $ARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)_{12}$, is employed (formalized in its standard
backshift-operator-based form):

$$
\Phi_P(B^{12})\,\phi_p(B)\,(1-B)^d\,(1-B^{12})^D\,y_t
= c + \Theta_Q(B^{12})\,\theta_q(B)\,\varepsilon_t,
\qquad \varepsilon_t \sim WN(0, \sigma^2),
$$

where $B$ is the backshift operator, $\phi_p$, $\theta_q$, $\Phi_P$, and
$\Theta_Q$ are the (seasonal) autoregressive and moving average polynomials,
and $d$ and $D$ are the orders of (seasonal) differencing. The orders are
selected automatically by the Hyndman-Khandakar algorithm implemented in
`forecast::auto.arima()` [3], [4], which determines $d$ and $D$ with
unit-root tests and then performs a stepwise search over $p$, $q$, $P$, and
$Q$ to minimize the corrected Akaike information criterion (AIC). The model
is estimated on the tibble `WORLD` for cases, deaths, and the mortality rate
(in percent) separately (see Table 3, Figure 3, and the R code below for
additional details).

```{r modelA, echo = TRUE, results = 'hide'}
models    <- WORLD                                                           %>%
             transmute(Cases = CASES, Deaths = DEATHS,
                      `Mortality rate (%)` = 100 * MORTALITY)                %>%
             map(\(y) auto.arima(ts(y, frequency = 12,
                                    start = c(year( min(WORLD$MONTH)),
                                              month(min(WORLD$MONTH))))))
forecasts <- map(models, forecast, h = 12)
```

```{r hidden4, include = FALSE}
ljung_box <- function(m) {                              # as in checkresiduals()
  res <- residuals(m)
  lag <- max(length(coef(m)) + 3, min(2 * frequency(res),
                                      round( length(res) / 5)))
  Box.test(res, lag = lag, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = length(coef(m)))
}
DIAG      <- tibble(
  Series  = names(models),
  Model   = sapply(models, as.character),
  AIC     = sapply(models, \(m) m$aicc),
  Q       = sapply(models, \(m) unname(ljung_box(m)$statistic)),
  DF      = sapply(models, \(m) unname(ljung_box(m)$parameter)),
  P       = sapply(models, \(m) ljung_box(m)$p.value)
)
FORECAST  <- imap(forecasts, \(f, s) tibble(
  SERIES  = s,
  MONTH   = max(WORLD$MONTH) %m+% months(1:12),
  VALUE   = as.numeric(f$mean),
  LOW80   = as.numeric(f$lower[, 1]), HIGH80 = as.numeric(f$upper[, 1]),
  LOW95   = as.numeric(f$lower[, 2]), HIGH95 = as.numeric(f$upper[, 2])
))                                                                           %>%
  bind_rows()                                                                %>%
  mutate(SERIES = factor(SERIES, levels = names(models)))
horizon   <- FORECAST                                                        %>%
  filter(MONTH == max(MONTH))                                                %>%
  select(SERIES, VALUE)                                                      %>%
  deframe()
seasonal  <- any(str_detect(DIAG$Model, "\\[12\\]"))
white     <- all(DIAG$P >= 0.05)
```

Following the model, the formal statistical test of **H3** is the Ljung-Box
test of the residuals, $H_0: \rho_1 = \cdots = \rho_h = 0$ (white noise)
against $H_1: \exists_{\rho_j}\ \rho_j \neq 0$, with $h$ and the degrees of
freedom chosen as in `forecast::checkresiduals()`. Table 3 comprises the
selected specification of each model, its AIC, and the Ljung-Box statistic
$Q$, degrees of freedom, and p-value. `auto.arima()` selected
`r DIAG$Model[1]` for cases, `r DIAG$Model[2]` for deaths, and
`r DIAG$Model[3]` for the mortality rate, i.e., all three series required
differencing, as anticipated in the analysis of time trends,
`r if (seasonal) "with seasonal components in at least one case" else
"while no seasonal components were selected"`. $H_0$ is
`r if (white) "not rejected" else "rejected for at least one series"` at the
5% significance level ($\alpha=0.05$), i.e.,
`r if (white) paste("the residuals of all three models are statistically",
"indistinguishable from white noise, supporting **H3**, ",
"i.e. making the Auto-ARIMA to be a good model choice") else
paste("residual autocorrelation remains in at least one model, which",
"weakens the support for **H3**")`.

```{r table3, echo = TRUE}
DIAG                                                                         %>%
mutate(P = scales::pvalue(P, accuracy = 0.001))                              %>%
knitr::kable(digits  = 3, format.args = list(big.mark = ",",
                                             scientific = FALSE),
             caption = "Selected ARIMA models and Ljung-Box tests")
```

Figure 3 depicts the 12-month forecasts (point forecasts with 80% and 95%
prediction intervals), which extrapolate the cumulative time series: by
`r format(max(FORECAST$MONTH), "%B %Y")`, the point forecasts amount to ca.
**`r number_fmt(round(horizon["Cases"]))` cases** and
**`r number_fmt(round(horizon["Deaths"]))` deaths**, with the **mortality
rate at `r round(horizon["Mortality rate (%)"], 2)`%** (versus
`r percent_fmt(mortality)` in `r m_max`), while the implied ratio of the
forecasted deaths to the forecasted cases declines to ca.
`r round(100 * horizon["Deaths"] / horizon["Cases"], 2)`%, since the
forecasted cases grow faster -- i.e., the three univariate models are not
mutually consistent. Given only `r nrow(WORLD)` monthly observations, the
prediction intervals widen rapidly with the horizon (for the mortality rate,
the lower bounds even become negative, since the Gaussian intervals ignore
the non-negativity of the ratio), and the forecasts should be interpreted as
a continuation of the most recent dynamics rather than a serious epidemiological
projection.

```{r figure3, echo = TRUE, fig.height = 3.2, fig.pos = "H"}
ggplot(WORLD                                                                 %>%
       transmute(MONTH, Cases = CASES, Deaths = DEATHS,
                `Mortality rate (%)` = 100 * MORTALITY)                      %>%
       pivot_longer(-MONTH, names_to = "SERIES", values_to = "VALUE")        %>%
       mutate(SERIES = factor(SERIES, levels = names(models))),
       aes(x = MONTH, y = VALUE))                                              +
  geom_ribbon(data = FORECAST, aes(ymin = LOW95, ymax = HIGH95),
              fill = "red", alpha = 0.15)                                      +
  geom_ribbon(data = FORECAST, aes(ymin = LOW80, ymax = HIGH80),
              fill = "red", alpha = 0.30)                                      +
  geom_line(data = FORECAST,  linewidth = 0.7,  color = "red")                 +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7)                                                   +
  facet_wrap(~SERIES, scales = "free_y", axes = "all_x",
                                         axis.labels = "all_x")                +
  scale_y_continuous(labels  = scales::comma)                                  +
  labs(
    title = paste0("Figure 3. ARIMA forecasts, ",
                   format(min(FORECAST$MONTH), "%b %Y"), "-",
                   format(max(FORECAST$MONTH), "%b %Y")),
    x = "Month",
    y = "Cumulative value (world)"
  )                                                                            +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Discussion of Potential Bias

The findings in the report, despite the use of rigorous methodology, are subject
to several potential biases, the first group of which is data-related. On the
one hand, both the numerator and the denominator of the mortality rate are
measured with error: COVID-19 deaths may have included deaths "with" rather than
"from" the disease (e.g., patients with severe comorbidities or other diseases,
since countries differed in whether a positive test alone sufficed for the
classification), while confirmed casescomprised false positives (imperfect
specificity of PCR and rapid antigen tests) and, far more importantly, omitted a
substantial share of undetected cases (asymptomatic or mild infections, limited
testing capacity, and individual home testing from 2022 onward). On the other
hand, monthly aggregation discarded the within-month variability in data.

The second group of potential biases is method-related, given that the three
hypotheses were tested with basic (textbook) procedures. First, the linear
trends in Table 1 were estimated on cumulative (integrated) series, which
violate the Gauss-Markov assumptions and inflate both the $R^2$ and the
significance of the slopes -- i.e., the trends are descriptive rather than
inferential. Second, Pearson's $\chi^2$ tests in Table 2 are based on counts
in the hundreds of millions, so that even thr smallest deviations are
statistically significant, i.e., the rejection of **H2** is practically
guaranteed (moreover, the expected counts of a few micro-states fall below
five). Third, the ARIMA models were estimated on only `r nrow(WORLD)` monthly
observations with structural breaks (new disease variants, vaccination, and/or
changes in mitigation policies), and the mortality rate was modeled directly as
a ratio rather than derived from its components. Hence, although these
limitations do not necessarily invalidate the obtained findings, they merit
further investigation (beyond the scope of this short report).

## Conclusion

This brief report examined `r number_fmt(total_cases)` confirmed COVID-19
cases and `r number_fmt(total_deaths)` deaths recorded by the Johns Hopkins
University CSSE in `r n_iso3` countries between `r m_min` and `r m_max` (a
world mortality rate of `r percent_fmt(mortality)`) and answered the three
research questions with formal statistical hypotheses tested at the 5%
significance level ($\alpha=0.05$). First, in terms of long-term trends (1),
the monthly series exhibited significant linear trends -- increasing for
cumulative cases and deaths and declining for the mortality rate, which
peaked at `r percent_fmt(peak$MORTALITY)` in
`r format(peak$MONTH, "%B %Y")` -- leading to acceptance of **H1** (see
Table 1), with the declining trend shared by `r n_neg` of the `r n_slopes`
countries. Second, in terms of the cross-country structure (2), cases and
deaths were concentrated in a few populous countries, while the highest
mortality rates were observed in countries with limited testing capacity
(see Figure 2), and Pearson's $\chi^2$ tests rejected both the uniform
distribution of cases and deaths and the proportionality of deaths to cases
(see Table 2), i.e., rejecting **H2**. Third, in terms of the time-series
model (3), `auto.arima()` selected `r DIAG$Model[1]`, `r DIAG$Model[2]`, and
`r DIAG$Model[3]` for cases, deaths, and the mortality rate, respectively,
with the Ljung-Box tests
`r if (white) "supporting" else "only partially supporting"` **H3** (see
Table 3), and the 12-month forecasts extrapolated the cumulative series,
with the mortality rate expected at ca.
`r round(horizon["Mortality rate (%)"], 2)`% by
`r format(max(FORECAST$MONTH), "%B %Y")` (see Figure 3). To sum up, in light
of the potential biases -- above all, the measurement error in both deaths
(which may have included other diseases) and cases (false positives and,
predominantly, undetected infections) -- the findings should be interpreted
with caution and subject to further investigation.
